title: Episode 51: The Kensington Runestone: The Medieval Nordic Riddle of Alexandria
description:
The Kensington Runestone: The Medieval Nordic Riddle of Alexandria: How a Swedish immigrant farmer unearthed a carved stone in the roots of an aspen tree, igniting a century of archaeological warfare. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of the American story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the autumn of 1898, a Swedish-American farmer named Olof Ohman was clearing timber on his homestead near Kensington, Minnesota, when his mattock struck a heavy gray slab clutched in the ancient roots of an aspen tree. Carved into its face and edge were sixty-five lines of medieval Scandinavian runes, describing an ill-fated Norse exploration party slaughtered on an island in the year 1362. Was the Kensington Runestone genuine proof of Vikings exploring the American heartland more than a century before Columbus, or was it the greatest Scandinavian hoax in frontier history? Here is George with the enduring mystery.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ROOTS OF THE ASPEN TREE
In November 1898, Olof Ohman, an industrious thirty-three-year-old immigrant from Forsa, Sweden, was clearing an elevated knoll on his farm in Solem Township, Douglas County, Minnesota. The region was a rolling landscape of glacial moraines, marshes, and oak groves settled heavily by Scandinavian homesteaders. While using a grubbing mattock to dislodge a stunted aspen tree, Ohman and his ten-year-old son Edward uncovered a two-hundred-and-two-pound slab of greywacke stone clutched tightly in the tree's primary roots. The main root was flattened against the rock, bearing witness that the stone had lain buried for decades. As Ohman wiped the glacial clay from the surface, he discovered strange geometric scratches carved into the broad face and along the narrow side edge. Recognizing them as ancient Nordic runes, Ohman displayed the rock in the window of the local bank in Alexandria, sparking immediate curiosity among his immigrant neighbors. The glacial knoll where Ohman worked was a solitary hill rising above ancient marshes that had once formed navigable waterways for native canoes centuries before. Ohman family had fled harsh economic conditions in Sweden, seeking freedom and opportunity on the fertile prairie soil of Douglas County with little thought of ancient Scandinavian history. The heavy grey slab had rested undisturbed beneath the roots of the aspen tree through centuries of prairie blizzards, prairie fires, and buffalo migrations across the rolling drumlins.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE 1362 INSCRIPTION
When scholars translated the runic text, they uncovered an astonishing and harrowing message. In transcribed fourteenth-century Norse dialect, the inscription read: 'Eight Goths and twenty-two Norwegians on an exploration journey from Vinland through the west. We had camp by two skerries one day's journey north from this stone. We were out and fished one day. After we came home, found ten men red with blood and dead. AVM save us from evil.' On the side edge, the inscription concluded: 'Have ten men by the sea to look after our ships, fourteen days' journey from this island. Year 1362.' The invocation 'AVM' was interpreted as the Latin Hail Mary: Ave Maria. If authentic, the inscription proved that a joint Swedish and Norwegian expedition had penetrated deep into the interior of North America via Hudson Bay and the Red River more than a hundred and thirty years before Christopher Columbus sighted the Caribbean. Ohman brushed away the damp earth with his thumb, marveling at the clean, rhythmic geometry of the carved runic characters incised into the hard greywacke stone. The inscription detailed a journey that spanned thousands of miles across uncharted oceans and boreal waterways, painting a harrowing picture of survival and death in the fourteenth-century wilderness. The text revealed deep terror and religious devotion, as medieval men facing sudden death in a remote continent etched their final prayers into the eternal stone for future generations to find. Early Scandinavian explorers were known to navigate inland waterways using shallow-draft longships, utilizing river networks across Eastern Europe and the North Atlantic with legendary seamanship.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE VERDICT OF THE ACADEMICS
The stone was shipped to the University of Minnesota and later to Northwestern University for evaluation by leading Scandinavian linguists. The initial academic reaction was swift and devastating. Professor George Curme and Scandinavian scholar Olaus Breda declared the inscription a clumsy modern forgery. They argued that several words—such as 'opdagelse' for discovery and English-sounding words like 'mans'—did not conform to standard fourteenth-century Old Norse grammar. Furthermore, they pointed out that the runes exhibited peculiarities unknown in classic medieval inscriptions. Humiliated and branded a frontier counterfeiter by academic authorities, Olof Ohman retrieved his heavy stone, took it back to his farm, and placed it face-down near his barn door to serve as a stepping stone, refusing to speak to journalists or scholars for years. Local Scandinavian settlers gathered on Sundays to examine the stone, debating whether their medieval ancestors had indeed navigated the great rivers of the northern continent. Scholars in Minneapolis and Chicago ridiculed the notion of Vikings navigating the Red River, insisting that the inscription must have been copied from modern Swedish encyclopedias. When the stone was returned to Ohman farm, neighbor boys used it as an anvil to straighten bent nails, completely indifferent to the academic debate raging in eastern universities. Academic skeptics demanded physical medieval iron weapons or settlement foundations, dismissing the lone boulder as an elaborate linguistic prank conceived by educated Scandinavian immigrants.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: ENTER HJALMAR HOLAND
The stone might have been lost to obscurity had it not been for a young Norwegian-American historian named Hjalmar Rued Holand. In 1907, Holand visited Ohman's farm to collect folklore for a history of Norwegian settlement. Fascinated by the runestone, Holand acquired it from Ohman and devoted the remaining fifty-five years of his life to defending its authenticity. Holand researched royal fourteenth-century archives in Scandinavia and discovered that King Magnus Eriksson of Sweden and Norway had indeed commissioned a high-ranking nobleman named Paul Knutson in 1354 to lead an expedition to Greenland and western territories to verify the religious orthodoxy of the Norse colonies. Holand argued that Knutson's expedition sailed southwest into Hudson Bay, ascended the Nelson and Red Rivers, and met disaster in the Minnesota lakes country in 1362, precisely matching the date and circumstances carved on the stone. Holand spent decades traveling between American universities and European archives, gathering sworn depositions from early pioneers who remembered the discovery of the stone. Holand spent years interviewing elderly Ojibwe and Dakota elders, collecting oral traditions of light-skinned men who had arrived in great wooden boats generations before the French fur traders. Holand mortgaged his own fruit farm in Wisconsin to finance his research trips, determined that the memory of the fourteenth-century Norsemen would not be erased by academic skepticism. Holand spent years traveling between remote homesteads, collecting sworn affidavits and diary entries from pioneer witnesses who had examined the stone when it was first pulled from the roots.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GEOLOGICAL CLUES
While linguists continued to feud over the grammar, geologists turned their microscopes toward the physical rock itself. The Minnesota Historical Society appointed state geologist Newton Horace Winchell to examine the weathering of the stone. Winchell conducted meticulous microscopic analyses of the carved rune grooves and compared them to the weathered natural edges of the greywacke boulder. He noted that the biotite and feldspar minerals exposed in the bottoms of the carved letters had undergone substantial chemical weathering that required at least fifty to a hundred years in the damp soil. Furthermore, extensive sworn depositions from local settlers confirmed that the aspen tree whose roots gripped the stone was between thirty and forty years old when cleared in 1898—predating white settlement in Douglas County, which only began in 1858. Microscopic petrographic analysis revealed that the weathering of the minerals inside the carved grooves matched the natural weathering of the stone outer surface. Winchell rigorous geological report concluded that the physical weathering of the greywacke boulder was consistent with centuries of exposure to damp soil rather than recent manufacture. Winchell spent weeks in the field examining the moraine topography, confirming that the knoll was once an island surrounded by glacial marshes in the fourteenth century, exactly as described on the stone. Modern laser surface scanning and microscopic mineral analysis have revealed complex chemical weathering inside the rune cuts that cannot be replicated by modern steel tools.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE 1362 DIALECT RESURFACES
Decades later, linguistic breakthroughs added fresh complexity to the mystery. In the mid-twentieth century, Swedish linguistic historians discovered obscure fourteenth-century manuscripts and regional dialects from Gotland and Dalarna that matched several of the exact lexical peculiarities previously deemed 'impossible' by nineteenth-century critics. The pentadic runic calendar numbers and unique runic variants carved on the Kensington stone, which nineteenth-century scholars believed had never existed, were found in genuine fourteenth-century parish records and medieval folk alphabets in rural Sweden. Critics counter-argued that Edward Larsson, a nineteenth-century Swedish schoolmaster, had preserved similar folk runes in a personal handbook. The battle lines hardened: either Ohman was an uneducated farmer who somehow possessed encyclopedic linguistic knowledge unknown to the world's greatest university professors, or the artifact was genuine. Linguists identified rare fourteenth-century Swedish idioms from Gotland that were unknown to modern dictionaries, supporting the authenticity of the ancient inscription. Rune carvers in medieval Scandinavia had developed specialized shorthand alphabets for secret parish correspondence, explaining the unusual characteristics that confounded nineteenth-century professors. Fourteenth-century Swedish manuscripts preserved in European archives contain several of the exact grammatical idioms and pentadic calendar runes once declared impossible by critics.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ENIGMA IN THE GRANITE HEART
Today, the Kensington Runestone resides in a secure, climate-controlled vault at the Runestone Museum in downtown Alexandria, Minnesota. More than a century after its discovery, it remains one of the most polarizing artifacts in world archaeology. Teams of modern geologists, equipped with laser scanners and electron microscopes, continue to debate the depth of weathering inside the runic grooves. Whether viewed as an epic testament to daring medieval Norse explorers who wept over fallen comrades in the Minnesota wilderness, or the most brilliant frontier intellectual riddle ever conceived by a Swedish homesteader, the Kensington Runestone remains an immortal American mystery that refuses to die. The museum in Alexandria attracts tens of thousands of visitors each year, who stand before the heavy grey stone and ponder the mysterious saga of America first European explorers. Today, visitors from across the globe gather in Alexandria, Minnesota, gazing upon the ancient stone and contemplating the extraordinary courage of fourteenth-century explorers who journeyed into the heart of an unknown continent.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The riddle of the Kensington Runestone continues to captivate scholars and explorers around the world. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we journey east into Wisconsin for the forgotten inferno that changed forestry forever: the Peshtigo Fire of 1871.
